1440.bp: Comics are everywhere—in print, online, streaming—but finding the one you're looking for is oddly hard. You can search by title or character name, sure, but what if you remember only the art style, the pacing of the story, or that the main character was a tough woman? Traditional search treats comics like simple text documents, missing everything that makes them special.
1440.wh: Comics pack three languages at once: pictures (backgrounds, character expressions, panel layout), words (dialogue and captions), and rhythm (how fast the story unfolds through panel size and composition). When you ask an AI to find what you like, it either retreats to text metadata or throws all the complexity into a neural network, leaving you wondering why it picked what it picked. Fans trust systems more when they can see the reasoning.
1440.ap: ESCOMIC watches what you actually click and hover over, learning which visual traits and story qualities matter most to you personally. It breaks down each comic into factual bits (genre, character gender, pacing speed) and visual patterns, then ranks results by combining all these signals. When you hover—a signal users give without thinking—the system quietly adjusts which factors to weight more heavily. Every result comes with a clear explanation: 'This one ranked high because it has the fast pacing you seemed to like, plus a confident female lead.'
1440.ww: Humans care about explanations because they want to know if a recommendation makes sense for them specifically. Fans who see why something ranked high can immediately judge whether to trust the system next time. The adaptive part works because people's tastes shift as they browse; a system that locks in one interpretation misses that drift. Showing the logic—not hiding it—builds confidence.
1440.po: In user tests with eye-tracking, people using ESCOMIC found better comics faster, felt more satisfied with results, and trusted the system more than standard search or opaque AI ranking. The effect is concrete: explicit explanation + personal adaptation = users actually using the tool instead of giving up.

1441.bp: Visual media—films, archives, security footage, medical imaging—lives everywhere, but searching it is fragmented and frustrating. You might use one tool for face recognition, another to find objects in a scene, a third for audio, and a fourth for metadata like dates. WISE asks: what if you could search all of these at once, in one place, without being a machine-learning engineer?
1441.wh: Each modality (images, video, audio, faces, text transcripts) has different technical requirements and specialized models. Tying them together into a single system that actually works fast enough and scales to millions of items is a massive engineering puzzle. Most people who need this are archivists, researchers, or security teams without the budget or expertise to wire up seven different systems.
1441.ap: WISE bundled together a collection of open retrieval models—one for object detection (finding 'horse' in any scene), one for face matching (finding that specific person), one for audio events (finding the 'wood creak' sound), one for scenes (finding 'empty street'). Each model lives in its own module. You can search by natural language ('show me trains in Germany'), by images you upload, or by audio samples. The results come back as a single ranked list, even though the search happened across totally different data types.
1441.ww: Vector search—converting images, audio, and text into points in a mathematical space where similar things cluster together—makes this practical at scale. Since each modality gets its own module, adding a new model later is straightforward: plug it in, and it works with everything else. The system is small enough to run locally, protecting private footage or sensitive archives from cloud exposure.
1441.po: Users can now ask questions they couldn't ask before: 'Find this face anywhere in our archive,' or 'Show me all scenes with German trains,' or 'Retrieve everything with that specific audio artifact.' The same system handles real-world collections from historical archives to security footage. No machine-learning background required.

1442.bp: Patents matter enormously to companies and researchers—they signal innovation, reveal technological directions, and help you spot threats and opportunities. But existing patent databases are shallow, listing basic facts like dates and inventors. For serious decisions about whether a patent is truly valuable or where a technology is headed, you need depth—understanding the real innovation, how it connects to other discoveries, and whether it's transformative or incremental.
1442.wh: A patent's real value isn't obvious from its title or abstract. You need to understand what the claimed invention actually does, how it differs from prior work, and how it sits within a web of related patents. Most R&D teams lack the time or expertise to assemble this picture manually. Large language models can help, but they generate summaries that still don't show you the connections or trends.
1442.ap: PatentMerit uses large language models to read and analyze patent text deeply, mapping where each patent sits in the landscape of technology clusters. It builds a visual network showing how patents cite each other—revealing genealogies and evolutionary paths. It tags patents with fine-grained classifications and identifies 'disruptive' ones (patents that break from the usual trajectory). It extracts key technical topics and generates written reports summarizing all this analysis.
1442.ww: Network visualization works because innovation doesn't happen in isolation—each patent builds on prior work and sparks later inventions. Seeing this web immediately reveals whether a technology is mature (many related patents over years) or emerging (sudden spike in citations). Identifying disruption mathematically—anomalies in the citation and classification networks—flags patents that genuinely change things, not just incremental tweaks.
1442.po: An R&D team can now ask: 'Is this a disruptive technology we should watch?' or 'How has this field evolved over five years?' or 'What technologies do we compete with or complement?' with concrete, justified answers. The system automates the cognitively heavy work of assembling a complete picture.

1443.bp: Searching documents using images and layout—not just text—is starting to matter. Imagine you're hunting through a thousand PDFs and you remember something about a table in the middle of page 5, or a specific diagram style. Traditional text search misses it entirely. 'Visual retrieval' systems that understand layout and design can find what you're after, but they generate thousands of vectors per document, making search prohibitively slow at scale.
1443.wh: Modern retrieval systems break each document page into visual patches and represent each patch as a vector. This captures layout and design details text-based search misses. The problem: a single page might produce 5,000 vectors, so searching a million-page collection means comparing billions of vectors, which is expensive and slow—sometimes impractical.
1443.ap: The Visual RAG Toolkit uses pooling—mathematically combining nearby vectors into single, denser summaries, the way you might take an average of neighboring pixels in an image. It creates two layers: a coarse layer with just a few dozen vectors per page for fast filtering, and a fine layer with full detail for a second pass of exact ranking. When you search, the system first uses the coarse vectors to quickly narrow to the most promising documents, then does precise matching only on those finalists.
1443.ww: This two-stage design mirrors how humans actually search: you skim quickly to eliminate obviously irrelevant pages, then read closely only what might be relevant. The pooling doesn't lose the information you need—it just compresses redundancy. Because this happens before any model training, you don't need to retrain the system for different documents, making it immediately practical.
1443.po: Document search runs about four times faster, using far fewer vectors in storage, while keeping the same accuracy. A person searching a large collection of technical PDFs or contracts now gets near-instant results without sacrificing the ability to find a diagram or table by its visual pattern.

1444.bp: Retrieval-augmented generation—augmenting large language models with relevant documents pulled from databases—is powerful but intimidating. Most people think you either need to be a machine-learning expert or pay cloud companies for managed services. EasyRAG asks: what if beginners could learn this hands-on, starting from the basics and building up intuition?
1444.wh: RAG involves many moving parts: finding the right documents, feeding them to the language model, deciding how to rank results, tuning speed versus quality. Tutorials jump straight to code without building intuition. Newcomers hit dead ends—unclear why retrieval failed, unsure whether their setup is reasonable, unable to debug problems without deep expertise.
1444.ap: EasyRAG layers learning in three stages. Level one uses APIs (Google Search, for example) as the retriever, so you see the core idea—fetch external knowledge, feed it to the language model—without infrastructure overhead. Level two implements three concrete, related methods side-by-side: Fusion-in-Decoder and its lighter variant, then Stochastic RAG, each extending the previous so you see where complexity buys you gains. Level three opens the door to full customization.
1444.ww: Teaching through concrete examples and progression is faster than abstract theory. Comparing methods side-by-side—all in the same codebase with the same data—makes the trade-offs visceral: using lighter retrieval is faster but slightly less accurate; end-to-end optimization is powerful but expensive. Starting with APIs lets people separate 'how does RAG work?' from 'how do I build an efficient retriever?'
1444.po: A beginner can now understand RAG deeply enough to deploy it and tune it for their own problem, without hiring a specialist. The progression means you build real intuition, not just copy a tutorial.

1445.bp: Nepali is spoken by 26 million people, yet there is no standardized test collection to systematically evaluate how well search systems work for Nepali speakers. This means researchers can't compare approaches, and companies can't benchmark improvements. Search quality for underserved languages stagnates because there's no common yardstick.
1445.wh: Building a rigorous test collection requires thousands of genuine search queries, relevant documents, and human judgments of what counts as a good match. For major languages like English, this work is funded and public (TREC collections, etc.). For Nepali—a low-resource language—funding and expertise are scarcer, and the quirks of Nepali grammar and script make the work harder to outsource.
1445.ap: This paper proposes a methodology for creating a Nepali IR benchmark that includes three scenarios: Nepali speakers searching in Nepali (monolingual), English speakers searching for Nepali results (cross-lingual), and speakers mixing Nepali and English in queries (code-mixed). The work identifies existing Nepali documents and would use native speakers to judge relevance.
1445.ww: A standardized benchmark works because everyone tests on the same data, making results comparable. Nepali's rich morphology—one word can take many forms—is actually valuable for research: methods that handle Nepali's complexity transfer well to other morphologically rich languages. Code-mixed queries reflect reality: many bilingual users switch between languages mid-query.
1445.po: With a public benchmark, researchers can rigorously develop and compare retrieval methods for Nepali. Companies can measure their progress. The infrastructure becomes reusable for related languages.

1446.bp: Hausa and Fongbe are spoken by millions in West Africa, yet information retrieval research for these languages is nearly nonexistent. When people search in these languages using systems designed for English, results are often irrelevant or wrong. Understanding what techniques (reranking, query expansion) actually help—or hurt—is foundational before building better systems.
1446.wh: Large language models work much better for some languages than others. Hausa, spoken by tens of millions, has more training data in LLMs than Fongbe, spoken by fewer. Query expansion—using an LLM to rephrase a search query—might help by clarifying intent, or it might confuse the system by injecting errors. You need rigorous experiments to know. And the data gap is huge: when you translate something into Fongbe, an LLM often produces gibberish.
1446.ap: This study directly compared several retrieval approaches: keyword-based search (BM25), multilingual dense retrieval (learned representations of meaning across languages), LLM-based reranking (using an LLM to score results), and LLM-based query expansion (asking the LLM to rephrase the query). They tested these on Hausa and Fongbe, using commercial LLMs, and measured both quality and the data characteristics.
1446.ww: The data reveals the mechanism: LLMs trained on English and high-resource languages transfer poorly to low-resource languages. Query expansion helps some problems (clarifying a confusing query) but hurts others (introducing errors when the LLM doesn't understand the target language well). Reranking—scoring existing results—is more robust than expansion because it doesn't inject new errors.
1446.po: The concrete finding: for Fongbe especially, straightforward multilingual dense retrieval often outperforms LLM-based expansion. This guides teams building real systems for these languages: invest in translation quality first; don't blindly assume LLM expansion helps. The benchmark and methodology open the door to iterative improvement.

1447.bp: People search in the languages they speak. When users query in Hindi, Bengali, or a mix of languages, search systems almost always interpret the query in English, often failing to find relevant results. Small language models are starting to serve as the 'smart router' layer in search pipelines, but they're almost always prompted in English, leaving linguistic diversity on the table.
1447.wh: Prompting an AI model in English when the user thought in their native language is a mismatch. The model might understand 'what is your name' better in English than in Hindi because it saw more English training data. But that doesn't mean English-only prompting is optimal—the model still understands Hindi, and asking in multiple languages might give it more angles to solve the problem.
1447.ap: This team prompts the same frozen language model in three languages—English, Hindi, and Bengali—on the exact same query classification task, then averages the results (weighting by the model's confidence in each language). No retraining, no translation, no extra data needed. They test nine models, from 1 billion to 9 billion parameters, on four benchmark datasets.
1447.ww: Different languages emphasize different aspects of meaning. A Hindi prompt might make certain query intents clearer; a Bengali prompt might catch nuances English misses. Averaging predictions across languages combines these perspectives without requiring the model to be fluent in all of them. The modest computational overhead (1.2–1.4 times slower) is worth it because classification accuracy jumps 3–5 percentage points.
1447.po: Query classification—routing a search to the right handler—now works measurably better for multilingual speakers without retraining or translation services. This matters in regions with widespread code-mixing (mixing languages in one sentence) and shows the technique scales to larger models.

1448.bp: Chichewa is spoken by 12 million people, but when someone wants to ask a database a question in Chichewa, there's a chasm: no systems exist. Text-to-SQL—converting natural language questions into database queries—works well in high-resource languages but has barely been explored for African languages. Bridging this gap unlocks database access for millions of people excluded from the digital economy.
1448.wh: Text-to-SQL is hard because a language model must understand both the natural language intent and the database schema. It's especially hard in Chichewa because there's almost no training data, and Chichewa's grammar is different from English (where most Text-to-SQL systems were trained). A model that works in English might stumble on Chichewa's structure.
1448.ap: This work first built a Chichewa Text-to-SQL dataset: 400 genuine questions paired with correct SQL queries, grounded in realistic data (agriculture, commodity prices, population). They then tested open-source language models with zero-shot (just asking), few-shot (showing examples), and retrieval-augmented (pulling relevant examples from the dataset) prompting, in both English and Chichewa. Finally, they fine-tuned selected models with QLoRA, a parameter-efficient method, and combined it with retrieval.
1448.ww: Retrieval-augmented prompting works because it retrieves similar examples from the limited Chichewa dataset; this acts like a teacher showing the model similar problems. QLoRA fine-tuning is crucial for low-resource settings because it's cheap (trains only a small set of parameters, not the whole model). The combination—retrieval showing patterns + fine-tuning adapting the model—narrows the accuracy gap from 56.7 percentage points (English-only) to 23.4.
1448.po: A Chichewa speaker can now ask database questions and get results, with 53.3% accuracy—a world of difference from zero. More concretely, farmers asking about commodity prices or weather conditions can get answers through a natural-language system trained with realistic low-resource techniques.

1449.bp: Rayalaseema, in southern India, is drought-stricken, and most farmers there are small landholders who need reliable agricultural advice—about water management, crop choice, drought coping. But this advice exists in English and Hindi, not Telugu, the language they speak. There are no question-answering datasets in Telugu for agriculture, so systems can't be built or evaluated.
1449.wh: Agricultural information retrieval for underserved regions requires more than translating English systems. Drought-specific advice (e.g., 'which crops survive with 300mm rain?') is locally critical but rarely in English. Farmer literacy is 60%, so systems must handle varied input (misspellings, short questions, rural dialect). Building a benchmark requires access to local experts and relevant materials.
1449.ap: This paper documents the gap: agricultural QA datasets exist in Hindi, Tamil, and Bengali, but not Telugu. It identifies available information sources (government extension materials, Kisan Call Center records—thousands of farmer calls recorded and transcribed). It proposes a methodology: extract questions from call center logs, pair them with authoritative answers from extension materials, validate with Telugu-speaking agriculturalists, and build a public benchmark.
1449.ww: Call center logs are gold because farmers ask real questions they actually need answered, not hypothetical ones. Local extension materials are authoritative and context-aware. A dataset built this way is immediately relevant to the deployment context—systems trained on it will handle the actual needs and language variations farmers use.
1449.po: Once built, this benchmark enables targeted development of Telugu agricultural QA systems. It serves 74 million Telugu speakers and creates a model for similar low-resource language + domain combinations (e.g., Marathi health information, Assamese fisheries).

1450.bp: Marathi speakers in India want timely information—news, local events, job postings—but large language models with built-in web search often fail to find relevant results in Marathi. The dream of 'talk to the web in your language' is undermined by gaps in search, retrieval quality, and how well LLMs handle low-resource languages.
1450.wh: Web-augmented LLMs are powerful in English but struggle in Marathi. The LLM might invoke a search tool multiple times, but if the web returns results in mixed language or the LLM misunderstands the results, the final answer is wrong. Testing this requires carefully designed queries that capture real user needs (not just translated global queries) and metrics that isolate what's failing: search retrieval, result integration, or language understanding.
1450.ap: MarathiWeb is a benchmark with two types of queries: global needs translated into Marathi (e.g., 'weather in London') and natively authored local needs (e.g., 'where can I buy fresh turmeric in Pune?'). Each query has golden-standard answers. They tested two frontier LLMs with web search against a Google-based retrieval baseline, and analyzed failure patterns and cost (how many web calls).
1450.ww: Local information retrieval is harder than global because fewer sources cover local topics in Marathi, and LLMs have even less training data. Separating translated queries from native ones matters because failure patterns differ: global queries fail due to language degradation; local queries often fail because sources don't exist. Shallow retrieval (one web call) beats deep multi-step search in Marathi, likely because each additional step introduces more opportunities for language understanding to fail.
1450.po: The benchmark exposes that LLM web search breaks down in Marathi, especially for local information. It provides both a diagnostic tool and a concrete challenge for improving low-resource language information access. The finding that shallow retrieval outperforms deep search is counterintuitive and actionable for system design.

1451.bp: Summarizing multiple documents in languages like Vietnamese, Thai, or Indonesian is useful for news aggregation, research synthesis, and decision-making. But large language models that generate summaries are too expensive to run on a single GPU in countries with limited compute infrastructure. Extractive summarization—picking the best existing sentences rather than generating new ones—is cheaper but needs to work across typologically diverse low-resource languages.
1451.wh: Abstractive summarization (generating new text) requires massive models. Extractive summarization (choosing existing sentences) avoids hallucination but is harder in low-resource languages because learning which sentences matter depends on language-specific understanding. Standard transformer models are expensive; you need a lightweight approach.
1451.ap: This team combined two technical ideas: mixture-of-experts embeddings (which adapt to different languages without retraining) and graph neural networks that model how sentences relate to each other (discourse structure). The full model has only 3.2 million trainable parameters—30 times smaller than typical transformer approaches—making it trainable on a single GPU in hours, not days.
1451.ww: Discourse structure matters: good summaries preserve the flow and connections between ideas, not just high-scoring sentences in isolation. Graph neural networks capture these relationships. Mixture-of-experts avoids training a separate model per language; a single model adapts to the linguistic properties of Vietnamese, Thai, etc. The small parameter count means the approach is truly accessible to resource-limited teams.
1451.po: Teams in Vietnam, Thailand, or Indonesia can now run the system locally on modest hardware, summarizing multi-document collections in their language without cloud cost or privacy concerns. The approach scales across unrelated language families (Austroasiatic, Kra-Dai, Austronesian), showing the technique generalizes.

1452.bp: When large language models generate answers to agricultural questions in Swahili, are they any good? How can you tell if an answer is reasonable versus nonsense? In low-resource settings, there's often no gold standard to compare against. Understanding whether LLM-generated answers are detectably different from human expert answers is a first step toward quality control.
1452.wh: LLMs sometimes hallucinate—they output plausible-sounding but false information. In Swahili agricultural IR, there's limited prior work to guide what 'quality' should look like. You can't always run human evaluations at scale. If LLM-generated answers have consistent, detectable patterns (e.g., always longer, always less diverse in word choice), you could use that as a signal for quality assessment.
1452.ap: This team collected 127 Swahili questions about maize and got answers from three sources: human agricultural experts, ChatGPT, and Gemini. They measured textual properties: answer length, lexical diversity (do they use varied vocabulary or repeat words?), and semantic similarity (how much do they overlap in meaning with human answers?). They then trained a classifier to predict whether an answer came from an expert, ChatGPT, or Gemini.
1452.ww: LLMs tend to output more uniform text than humans. A person answers a question directly; an LLM often elaborates, hedges, and rambles. These patterns—longer length, lower diversity, moderate semantic overlap—are mathematical signatures. A classifier learns these signatures because LLMs are trained on vast text that differs from how a specific expert in Swahili agriculture speaks.
1452.po: You can now automatically flag likely LLM-generated answers as needing human review, without building an expert panel for every query. The 98% classification accuracy suggests this approach could be practical for quality assurance in low-resource agricultural IR systems.

1453.bp: Machine translation from English into Tetun (Timor-Leste) or Bislama (Vanuatu) is often mediocre because training data is sparse and highly skewed toward general text, not medical or disaster relief terminology. But local health workers and disaster response teams need accurate translation of urgent information. They don't have time to fix machine errors; they need systems that 'just work' in their domain.
1453.wh: Generic machine translation uses data mostly about politics and social topics, making medical terminology a weak point. A small team in Timor-Leste can't afford to collect thousands of domain-specific sentence pairs to retrain a full model. They need a system that leverages limited in-domain resources without massive retraining.
1453.ap: Tulun combines standard neural machine translation with retrieval and large language model post-editing. When you translate a medical sentence, the system retrieves similar examples from a small, curated in-domain memory (translation glossaries and examples specific to medicine), shows these to the LLM, and asks the LLM to review and improve the translation. Users can add their own domain-specific terms and examples, which are immediately used in subsequent translations.
1453.ww: This design is practical because in-context learning—showing an LLM examples from your specific domain—works without retraining. Retrieval means you only show the LLM relevant examples, keeping the prompt focused. User-configurable glossaries mean the system adapts to local terminology. The transparency (showing users which examples guided the translation) builds trust.
1453.po: Medical translation accuracy improved 16–22 points over baseline MT without needing expensive retraining. Disaster relief teams in Vanuatu and health workers in Timor-Leste now have a tool that adapts to their needs in real time and they can see why translations were chosen, allowing them to correct and improve the system.

1454.bp: Shona is spoken by 12 million people in Zimbabwe and Southern Africa, yet retrieval research almost never addresses it. Shona has rich morphology—one root word takes many prefixes and suffixes that change meaning—which makes retrieval harder than for languages like English. Building a retrieval system for Shona requires understanding these morphological patterns and having a benchmark to test against.
1454.wh: Standard retrieval methods treat each word form as separate. In Shona, 'to go', 'going', 'went', 'will go', and 'should have gone' are all variations of one root; treating them as different words means the system misses relevant documents. Solving this requires morphology-aware processing, but development is blocked without a benchmark—no public test set for Shona retrieval exists.
1454.ap: This work ran initial experiments using standard sparse retrieval (BM25) and dense retrieval on Shona text, demonstrating significant performance gaps compared to English. Based on these findings, it proposes a plan to build a large-scale Shona IR benchmark and develop methods aware of Shona's morphological structure.
1454.ww: Morphology-aware retrieval works because it groups related word forms, connecting 'going' and 'went' as variations of the same concept. A benchmark is essential because it lets you measure whether morphological processing actually helps and provides a standard for comparing approaches. Building this foundation for Shona is a step toward equitable IR across language families.
1454.po: Once a Shona IR benchmark and morphology-aware methods are in place, the system can handle the full range of how people naturally speak Shona. This work charts a path for similar effort on other morphologically rich low-resource languages, advancing digital inclusion and equitable access to information technology.
